title: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear
description: Edmund Hamilton Sears's Christmas carol to Richard Storrs Willis's tune "Carol", in Willis's four parts as Charles L. Hutchins printed them in 1916, for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1 to 3 in a gentle six-eight. At "Peace on the earth" the tune falls an octave and climbs back step by step, then the last line comes home like the first.

credits.tune: "Carol", Richard Storrs Willis (1850, full form by 1869)
credits.arrangement: Richard Storrs Willis's four parts (as printed by Charles L. Hutchins, 1916), adapted by Stackapella

licence.arrangement: Willis's four parts as printed in Carols Old and Carols New (credited "R. S. Willis"; Willis died 1900; the book's editor Charles L. Hutchins died 1920; public domain): his tune unchanged in his key and metre, and his chords, with these changes for 2 to 4 beginners: every lower part sings one note a syllable where Willis moves within one (6 places: the bass under "glo-", the tenor under "harps", "earth" in "Peace on the earth", "heav'n's", "gra-" and "an-"); on "old" the alto takes A4 and the tenor C4 (his F4 and A3), so the duet has the F chord's third; on the next "From" the tenor sings A3 and the bass F2 (his F3 and F3), so the bass line has one leap of a fifth, not two; on "Peace on" the alto sings F-sharp 4 and the tenor A3 (his D4 and D3, the four parts in octaves), so every size has the D chord's third and the tenor no minor-sixth leap from "gold"; the bass sings G2 on "men" (his G3), so it has no leap of a sixth into "From"; on "cious" and "King" the alto steps down C4 and A3 (his E4 and F4, a unison with the tune) and the tenor sings F3 on "King" (his A3), so the duet has a sixth; on the pickup "The" the alto sings C4 (his E-flat 4, a tritone from A3), so that chord is F, not F7, and the bass F2 (his F3), as at "From"; verses 2 and 3 sung to the same parts; breaths written in for beginners at Willis's couplets (the held notes of "old", "gold" and "King" give up half a beat), with a bar's rest between verses; the bass sings G2 under "on", "bend-" and "sol-" (beat 2 of each verse's first and third lines) and A2 under "heav'n's" with the tenor on C4, so the trio has each chord's third; the alto takes D4 on each verse's pickup "The" into its third line. Accepted exceptions: Willis's alto holds D4 with the tune's lowest note on "the earth", so the duet sings a unison and the trio has no third there (the tenor keeps F#3 at 4 singers), and the duet has a bare fourth, G4 over D4, on "will": the only third would put the alto above the tune; and the duet's bare fifth on "heav'n's", where the tune's A comes on "all" and the alto's F4 falls to E4.
licence.source: Charles L. Hutchins, Carols Old and Carols New (Boston: The Parish Choir, 1916; the page footed "Parish Choir, No. 1843-4"), Carol 607, "It came upon the midnight clear", p. 491, "Words by Rev. E. H. Sears", "R. S. Willis", in four parts in B-flat, 6/8, written here in B-flat in 6/8 as printed (a dotted crotchet to the beat); verses 1 and 2 as printed under the music and verse 3 ("O ye, beneath life's crushing load", Hutchins's "O ye" where Sears printed "And ye") as printed below it, fitted to the notes by us as verses 1 and 2 are ("swiftly" where the plate reads "swiftiy"); Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy, read from the scan at archive.org/details/carolsoldcarolsn00huth/page/n522; compared with the earliest known printing of the words with this tune, Hymns and Songs of Praise for Public and Social Worship, ed. Roswell D. Hitchcock, Zachary Eddy and Philip Schaff (New York, 1874; preface dated 20 March 1874; music edited by John K. Paine and U. C. Burnap, assisted by James Flint), No. 158, "Christmas Carol", tune "CAROL. C. M.", p. 66, credited "Richard Storrs Willis", in B-flat in 6/8, its chords the same where compared (its third line starts on D over F, where Hutchins has F over F), at archive.org/details/hymnssongso00hitc/page/n73; "hovering" sung as "hov'ring" on its two notes, as the print sets it.
